claims.text: Boride-based substrates are commonly used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
A dense 1–2 µm Al2O3 overlayer will significantly improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
PVD can be used to form a continuous, low-porosity protective coating on the proposed substrate.
Thermal spraying can produce the proposed continuous, low-porosity 1–2 µm Al2O3 coating.
Approximately 660–750 °C represents typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures.
The Al2O3 overlayer will remain thermally stable during extended exposure to molten aluminum at approximately 660–750 °C.
A continuous alumina overlayer will prevent direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The alumina film will act as a diffusion barrier.
The proposed diffusion barrier will limit chemical reaction between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The proposed diffusion barrier will limit interdiffusion across the coating/substrate system.
The proposed diffusion barrier will limit dissolution of the boride substrate into molten aluminum.
Coated specimens will exhibit lower mass loss than equivalent uncoated boride specimens under the same molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated components will have a longer service lifetime than uncoated boride components.
Coating flaws or pores exceeding approximately 1% of the coating area may reduce protection.
Operation near or above 800 °C may reduce the coating's protection.
Mechanical damage that compromises coating integrity may reduce corrosion protection.
Matched coated and uncoated coupons exposed at 700–750 °C for up to 500 h provide a controlled test of the hypothesis.
Mass change can be used to quantify corrosion rate in the proposed molten-aluminum test.
Cross-sectional microscopy can assess coating integrity and substrate dissolution.
Failure of coated specimens to show both lower mass loss and superior mechanical integrity relative to uncoated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
